messages.text: I'm 4 months pregnant and live alone. I make $3,000 a month. Can I get WIC?

You probably can get WIC (the Women, Infants, and Children nutrition program). I'd call it **likely**, and I'd encourage you to apply.

**Why**
- WIC's income limit is 185% of the federal poverty level, and income is counted before taxes.
- A pregnant woman is usually counted as 2 people, because the unborn baby counts. The WIC rules I found from other states say this. I couldn't open Tennessee's own policy, so a clinic will confirm it.
- For 2 people, the 2026–27 limit is about **$3,337 a month**, or $40,034 a year. Your $3,000 a month is under that.
- If your baby weren't counted, the limit for 1 person is about **$2,461 a month**, and you'd be over it. So this counting rule matters. You can ask the clinic to count your baby, and they'll apply it.
- If you're expecting twins or more, tell them. Each baby counts, and the limit is higher.
- Being pregnant also meets WIC's health-and-nutrition requirement. A clinic staff member will do a short health check, which is usually quick.

**What to do next**
- **Website:** The Tennessee Department of Health runs WIC. You can start at tn.gov/health and search for "WIC".
- **Phone:** I couldn't confirm the current number. Call **211** and they'll connect you to your local WIC clinic.
- Bring proof of your pregnancy and your recent pay stubs.

**Other programs**
- Your income may be too high for food assistance (SNAP) alone. You can still apply, and I can check it for you.
- Pregnancy coverage through TennCare (Tennessee's Medicaid) has higher income limits than most people expect. I can check that for you too.

**Sources**
- [USDA WIC income guidelines, 2026–27](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/wic-ieg2026-2027.pdf) and [Federal Register notice](https://www.fna.usda.gov/wic/fr-042926). I could only see summaries of these, not the full tables.
- [Virginia WIC chart](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/content/uploads/sites/42/CRT-05.2.6.pdf), which has the 2-person figures (the same federal table).
- [Tennessee WIC income guidelines](https://www.tn.gov/health/health-program-areas/fhw/wic/income-guidelines.html). The page wouldn't open for me, and search results suggest it may still show last year's table.
- [Minnesota WIC manual](https://www.health.mn.gov/docs/people/wic/localagency/program/mom/chsctns/ch5/sctn5_2_4.pdf), which explains counting the unborn baby.

This is only an estimate. Only the WIC office can decide if you qualify.

Do you want me to check TennCare and food assistance (SNAP) next? If so, how much is your rent, and do you pay for heating or cooling separately?
Yeah, rent is $1,000. Heating/cooling I pay separately, but I don't know the exact amount yet. Sure, check SNAP and TennCare, thanks.

**Short answer:** TennCare looks **likely**. Food assistance (SNAP) looks **unlikely**, but you can still apply.

**TennCare (health coverage while pregnant): likely**
- TennCare covers pregnant women with income up to about **250% of the federal poverty level**. A TennCare notice says this. Dollar figures I found for a household of 2 run roughly $4,500 to $4,600 a month, but those come from secondary sites, so treat them as approximate.
- Your $3,000 a month is under that limit. It is under it even if the baby isn't counted.
- Coverage usually lasts through your pregnancy and 12 months after.
- **Apply:** tn.gov/tenncare or **1-855-259-0701**.
- CoverKids is for children, so it would matter for your baby after birth. TennCare is the route for you now.

**Food assistance (SNAP): unlikely**
- USDA's 2026–27 numbers for one person are about **$1,729 a month** at the old 130% limit and about **$2,660** at the 200% limit. Reports say Tennessee moved to 200%, but sources disagree on when. I couldn't settle that.
- Your $3,000 income before taxes is above both limits for a household of 1.
- SNAP normally doesn't count an unborn baby. If Tennessee did count the baby, the 200% limit would be about $3,600. Even then, I estimate your income after deductions would still be too high. I used 20% off your pay, a standard deduction, and rent plus a standard utility amount. That is why this looks unlikely rather than certain.
- I couldn't find Tennessee's official heating and cooling allowance. My estimate used a figure of about $358, which I couldn't verify. Your real bills won't change this much.
- Things could change after your baby is born. A household of 2 has a higher limit, and your costs may change too. You can reapply then.
- **You can still apply.** Only the state decides. Apply at **ONE DHS** (the Tennessee Department of Human Services' online portal) or call **211** for the DHS number.

**WIC** is still your best food help right now, as we covered.

**Sources**
I couldn't open the official pages. They blocked me, so these figures come from search summaries, and a caseworker should confirm them.
- [USDA SNAP 2026–27 cost-of-living memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)
- [Tennessee SNAP policy brief](https://sycamoretn.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap-in-tennessee.pdf)
- [TennCare pregnant women notice](https://www.TN.gov/content/dam/tn/tenncare/documents2/PregnantWomenComprehensiveNotice.pdf)
- [TennCare eligibility guide](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html)

Local help is free at **211**. Please report your income and household accurately on every application. Mistakes can lead to overpayments you'd have to pay back.

The Tennessee WIC limits for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 are 185% of the federal poverty guidelines, and the federal 2026-2027 figures match them.

- **Federal figures:** The USDA's 2026-2027 table lists a household of 1 at $29,526 annual and $2,461 monthly, and 4 at $61,050 annual and $5,088 monthly for the reduced-price meals column, which is the 185% level WIC uses.
- **Tennessee's rule:** Income eligibility for the Tennessee WIC Program is uniform statewide. Household gross income must be equal to or less than 185% of the federal poverty level.
- **Household sizes:** One third-party calculator lists the 2026 monthly limits from $2,461 for one person up to $8,590 for eight people, with each additional person adding $876 per month.
- **Discrepancy:** The Tennessee Department of Health page I found still shows the table for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026, so the state's own 2026-2027 table may not yet be posted there. Check the state page or your local health department before relying on the figures.

The results confirm the July 1, 2026 WIC guidelines and the 185 percent standard, but none of the sources I found reproduce the full 2026–2027 table.

- **Effective date and period:** USDA says the revised guidelines are effective July 1, 2026 and cover the period of July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027.
- **Income limit:** WIC eligibility follows the school-meals standard, and the income limit is 185 percent of the Federal poverty guidelines, as adjusted. The annual poverty-guideline revision behind these figures was published by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) at 91 FR 1797, on January 15, 2026.
- **Floor on state rules:** States cannot set WIC limits above the school-meals level or less than 100 percent of the federal poverty guidelines.
- **Example from a state agency:** Idaho's WIC program says a family of three can earn up to $50,542 a year under the new limits (up from $49,303). That figure is Idaho's published example, so I haven't checked it against the federal table.
- **Prior year for comparison:** The 2025–2026 table listed a 185 percent annual limit of $28,953 for a one-person household in the 48 contiguous states, based on the 2025 poverty guideline. (Effective from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026)

For exact 2026–2027 figures by household size, use the full USDA Federal Register notice (91 FR 23050, April 29, 2026), which I could only see in part.

The search didn't turn up an official Tennessee Department of Health WIC policy document on this point. The Tennessee-specific results are secondary websites, and the rule they describe matches the federal framework used by other states.

- **Tennessee guides:** One site says a pregnant woman should count her unborn child as a household member, and that Tennessee's income limit is 185% FPL. Another says households earning at or below 185% of the federal poverty level qualify. Neither cites a Tennessee policy manual, so check the Tennessee Department of Health WIC program directly before relying on them.
- **Federal-based rule in other state manuals:** Minnesota's WIC manual says a pregnant woman should be counted as two or more, taking into account the number of unborn fetuses. Iowa's manual describes a process where the applicant increases her household size by the number of expected births and then has income assessed using that adjusted size.
- **Opt-out:** Iowa's manual says a pregnant woman must be given the option of whether or not to count her unborn baby before delivery. Oregon's manual says the woman can waive this increase in household size if she wishes.
- **Multiple pregnancies:** Oregon's manual says that each fetus counts as an additional household member.

Overall, the sources agree that the unborn child counts toward household size for WIC income purposes. Whether Tennessee follows the same opt-out and multiple-fetus rules is not confirmed by these results.

- **Income limits:** The memo's 100% poverty table gives a net monthly limit of $1,330 for one person and $2,750 for four in the 48 states and D.C. - **Minimum benefit:** It rises from $24 to $25 for one- and two-person households in the contiguous states and D.C. ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/snap-benefits-are-increasing-october-1-new-payment-amounts-revealed-12393704)).
- **Deductions:** Coverage says several deductions also increase ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/snap-benefits-are-increasing-october-1-new-payment-amounts-revealed-12393704)), but I found no exact FY 2027 figures for the standard or shelter deductions.

Tennessee appears to have moved to a 200% gross income test, but the sources conflict on timing and on exact dollar figures, so verify with TDHS before relying on them.

- **Policy change:** A June 2026 article says the Tennessee Department of Human Services adopted broad-based categorical eligibility, raising the gross income threshold from 130% to 200% of the federal poverty level and removing asset limits for some households. Another puts the family-of-four limit at $62,400/year ($5,200/month) and cites USDA 2026 poverty guidelines. The gap is likely due to different poverty-guideline years, so the numbers should be checked against the official table.
- **Net income test:** Both tests generally apply. Net income must fall at or below 100% FPL. Households with someone 60 or older, or with a qualifying disability, are exempt from the gross income test.

Bottom line: the 200% gross limit under BBCE is reported by several sources, but the June 2026 adoption and the exact monthly figures should be confirmed directly with Tennessee DHS or the USDA FNS poverty-guideline tables.

Most sources agree that TennCare covers pregnant women with household income up to 250% of the federal poverty level, but they differ on the exact figure and on CoverKids.

- **The official figure is 250% FPL.** A TennCare notice says TennCare's income threshold for pregnant women was raised to 250 percent of the federal poverty level effective January 1, 2024. Earlier, the threshold was 195 percent of the federal poverty level.
- **Some 2026 guides show a slightly higher number.** Talktomira says limits include the 5% income disregard, so they run 5 points above the percentages Tennessee prints on its own chart. On that basis its pregnancy figure is 255% FPL, versus the 250% in the state's own materials.
- **Dollar figures for 2026.** CoveredUSA lists $54,100 per year for a pregnant woman (who is counted as a household of 2, herself and her unborn child), $68,300 for a household of 3, or $82,500 for a household of 4. Talktomira's monthly figure for a household of two is $4,599, which reflects the 255% limit.
- **Coverage length.** Pregnant enrollees are covered for the duration of their pregnancy and for 12 months following the end of pregnancy.
- **CoverKids is not a pregnancy pathway in most sources.** Talktomira describes it as covering children under 19 with family income up to 255% of the poverty line, and CoveredUSA describes it as covering children after birth. One checkmedicaid page says CoverKids covers children and pregnant women, but I'd treat that as the outlier. Pregnant women are generally routed through TennCare itself.
- **Source quality.** The official TennCare notice is the most authoritative source, though it is from 2023. The 2026 guides are secondary. Their poverty-level dollar amounts depend on which year's guidelines they use, so confirm current figures with TennCare at 1-855-259-0701 or tn.gov/tenncare.

The search did not turn up Tennessee's FY2027 SNAP standard utility allowance figures, so I can't give you the heating/cooling amount. The results give general background on how SUAs work.

- **Federal framework:** A final rule published November 18, 2024 finalizes changes proposed October 3, 2019, by the Department to revise SNAP regulations for calculating standard utility allowances and expand allowable shelter expenses to include basic internet costs.
- **State methodology:** State agencies must submit their SUA methodologies to FNS for approval at least every five years.
- **Timing:** FNS encouraged states to include basic internet costs with SUA values starting on October 1, 2025, because states typically update SUAs and cost-of-living adjustments at that time each year. That suggests the FY2027 values would take effect around October 1, 2026, but none of these results confirm Tennessee's figures.
- **Heating/cooling standard:** The HCSUA is the largest standard. Under the proposed methodology, it would be set at the 80th percentile of low-income households' utility costs in the State.

For the actual Tennessee FY2027 numbers, I'd check the Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP policy manual or its published SUA table, or the USDA FNS SUA page. A follow-up search aimed at the Tennessee DHS site would be the next step.
